case noun

in grammar

also cases, grammatical case, what case is it?, what case is this?, in what case?, oblique case, what case does it take?

classical

Quint. 1.5.47: in participiō per genus et cāsum … peccātur
Varr. LL 8.16 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 221, 245

cāsus, cāsūs m.

noun, fourth declension · Declension on Wiktionary

a grammatical case

Literally a “fall”, after Greek πτῶσις. The case of a word is asked in the ablative, Quō est cāsū?, and answered Ablātīvō (Traupman 238). The nominative and vocative are the “upright” cases, cāsūs rēctī; the rest are oblique, oblīquī (Varr. LL 8.49; Quint. 1.5.61 rēctō cāsū). Traupman’s Cui cāsuī servit?, what case does it take? (242), uses servīre in a sense not found in Lewis & Short.

Examples

  • in participiō per genus et cāsum, ut in vocābulō, per tempora, ut in verbō, per numerum, ut in utrōque, peccātur

    in the participle one goes wrong in gender and case, as in a noun, in tense, as in a verb, and in number, as in bothQuint. 1.5.47

  • alia cāsūs habent et rēctōs et oblīquōs

    some words have both upright and oblique casesVarr. LL 8.49 (Lewis & Short s.v. oblīquus)

  • Quō est cāsū?

    In what case is it?Traupman 238

  • Cāsūs nōminum quot sunt?

    How many cases of nouns are there?Traupman 221

  • Cui cāsuī servit?

    What case does it take?Traupman 242

See also nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative, ablative, declension, noun.
